title: Signs Your Attic Insulation Needs Replacing
h1: What Are the Signs Your Attic Insulation Needs Replacing?
description: Hot rooms, rising bills, thin or matted insulation and rodent or water damage are signs your attic insulation needs replacing. Here is what to look for.
quick_answer: Your attic insulation probably needs replacing if rooms are hard to keep comfortable, energy bills keep creeping up, you can see the tops of the ceiling joists, the insulation is flattened, clumped or stained, or it's been contaminated by rodents or water. Insulation that's damaged or full of droppings should be removed, not just covered over.
body:
Attic insulation doesn't last forever. It settles, gets crushed, soaks up leaks and becomes a home for rodents. In many older Southern California homes, the attic still has the original insulation from when the house was built, and it's often far thinner than it should be.

What signs show up inside the house?

You'll often feel insulation problems before you see them:

  • Upstairs or top-floor rooms that get very hot in summer, especially in inland areas
  • Rooms that cool off quickly on winter nights
  • An AC or furnace that seems to run constantly without keeping up
  • Energy bills that climb even though your habits haven't changed
  • Ceilings that feel warm to the touch on hot afternoons
  • Drafts around light fixtures, the attic hatch or ceiling vents

What should I look for in the attic?

Take a flashlight up to the hatch and check these:

  1. Depth. If you can see the tops of the ceiling joists, the insulation is probably too thin.
  2. Uneven coverage. Bare spots, piles and gaps around the edges let heat move freely.
  3. Compression. Insulation that's been walked on or had boxes stored on it loses much of its effectiveness.
  4. Water stains or dampness. Wet insulation stops working and can lead to mold.
  5. Rodent damage. Tunnels, nests, droppings and a urine smell mean the insulation is contaminated.
  6. Dark or dirty patches. Insulation can act like a filter. Dark areas often show where air is leaking up from the house.
  7. Old materials. Loose, pebble-like gray or gold insulation may be vermiculite, which can contain asbestos. Don't disturb it. Have it tested first.

How much attic insulation does a San Diego home need?

Insulation is measured by R-value, which describes how well it slows heat flow. Higher is better. U.S. Department of Energy recommendations for our climate start around R-30 for attics, and many homes benefit from more, especially in hotter inland areas.

Older homes often have far less than that. A professional can measure what you have and tell you how much it would take to bring it up to a better level.

Can I add new insulation on top of the old?

Sometimes. If the existing insulation is dry, clean and simply thin, adding more on top is often fine. But if it's wet, moldy, or contaminated with droppings and urine, it should come out first. Covering it traps the problem and the odor.

It's also smart to air seal before adding insulation. Sealing gaps around wiring, plumbing, light fixtures and the top plates of walls stops air from carrying heat and dust through the insulation.

What does insulation replacement involve?

A typical job looks like this:

  1. Inspect the attic and measure existing insulation
  2. Remove old or contaminated insulation with a high-powered vacuum system
  3. Sanitize the attic if there was rodent activity
  4. Seal air leaks between the house and attic
  5. Repair or seal ductwork while the attic is open
  6. Install new blown-in or batt insulation to the target R-value

Timing can help too. Spring and fall are comfortable seasons to work in the attic, and finishing before the inland summer heat or winter cold means you feel the difference right away. If rodents or a roof leak caused the damage, fix those first so the new insulation stays clean and dry.

Our attic insulation team handles removal, cleanup, air sealing and new insulation. You can check our specials page for current offers.

Ask for photos before and after the work, and ask what R-value the new insulation will reach. Blown-in insulation should also have depth markers stapled to the framing so you can check the coverage yourself later. That gives you a simple way to confirm the job reached the depth on your estimate.

Why does insulation matter so much with attic ducts?

In most Southern California homes, the ducts and often the furnace sit in the attic. On a hot day, that attic can be far hotter than outside. Good insulation keeps that heat out of your rooms, and sealed, insulated ducts keep the cool air inside them on its way to each room.
faqs: How long does attic insulation last?

Insulation can last for decades if it stays dry and undisturbed. Settling, foot traffic, leaks and rodents shorten its life. Many older homes have insulation that's thinner than when it was installed.
Will new insulation lower my energy bills?
Better insulation reduces how much heat moves through the ceiling, so your AC and furnace don't work as hard. How much you save depends on what you have now and how much you run your system.
Is blown-in or batt insulation better for an attic?
Both work. Blown-in insulation fills gaps and irregular spaces well and is common in attics. Batts work well in open, evenly spaced framing. The right choice depends on your attic layout.
Can I replace attic insulation myself?
Adding clean batts is a manageable project for some homeowners. Removing contaminated insulation is not. It requires protective gear, proper equipment and safe disposal.
